opus-5.5.text:
I think what's striking is how uneven it is, and how fast that unevenness is changing. A couple of years ago the obvious place you'd see impact was software engineering, because code is so verifiable. You can run it, you can test it, and the models got really good really quickly in that loop. Now we're seeing a similar pattern ripple outward into fields that have some notion of checkable correctness: mathematics, parts of the physical sciences, certain kinds of data analysis.

What I find most exciting is when you start seeing it in places where people didn't expect it to be useful yet. You'll hear from a researcher in biology or materials science who says, "I used this to sanity-check a derivation," or "it suggested an experiment I hadn't considered." These aren't moments where the model replaces the expert. They're moments where it becomes a real collaborator, and the expert's judgment becomes more important, not less.

The other thing I'd say is that adoption isn't just a function of capability. It's also about trust and workflow. In medicine or law, the bar for reliability is very high, and rightly so, so the diffusion looks slower and more careful. That's healthy. Our job is to keep pushing on reasoning and reliability so that the models earn that trust, and to work with practitioners to understand where they actually help.

So my mental model is less a single wave and more a set of frontiers. Each profession hits its own inflection point when the models cross a threshold that matters for that domain. We're watching a lot of those thresholds get crossed at once right now, and I think the next few years are going to be pretty remarkable.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI spreading unevenly across fields and gives examples, but does not characterize advances across nearly every profession as “Move 37”-like breakthroughs.

r002.rationale: It describes models as collaborators, but does not say AI agents can perform long-horizon work in people’s professions.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that the breakthroughs don't spread evenly. They spread first into whatever domain has the tightest feedback loop between the model and the ground truth.

Math and competitive programming went first for a reason. You can verify an answer. A proof either checks or it doesn't, a program either passes the tests or it doesn't, so you can train against that signal at enormous scale. That's why we saw models go from struggling with grade-school word problems to gold-medal-level performance on olympiad problems in a surprisingly short window. The capability wasn't magic. It was the availability of a verifier.

Software engineering came next, and it's the field where I think the diffusion is most visible to ordinary people, because every developer now has some agentic tool sitting next to them. Again, the reason is verifiability. You can run the code. You can run the test suite. The model can iterate against reality without a human in the loop.

The harder cases are the fields where the feedback is slow or noisy. Medicine, law, scientific research, policy. There, the question of "was that a good answer" might take months to resolve, or it might be a matter of judgment with no clean label. So the models are often already quite capable in those domains in a raw-knowledge sense, but the professions themselves adopt more cautiously, and the tooling to put the model in a real workflow is less mature.

What I find really interesting is that this is starting to change. The reasoning models generalize better than people expected. Skills learned on math and code seem to transfer into chemistry, into biology, into economics, places where we didn't explicitly train against a verifier. So I'd expect the next wave to be the model acting as a genuine collaborator in research, generating hypotheses, running experiments in simulation, reading the whole literature in a way no single human can.

The honest caveat is that the bottleneck for most professions is no longer the model. It's trust, integration, and the institutional willingness to change how work gets done. The capability is ahead of the adoption almost everywhere, and the gap between the two is where most of the interesting action is right now.

r001.rationale: The response describes uneven adoption and capability across fields, but does not characterize breakthroughs across nearly every profession as “Move 37”-like.

r002.rationale: It mentions agentic tools and future research collaboration, but does not state that AI agents can perform long-horizon work in people’s professions.

astra-6.text:
I think what’s exciting is that AI is becoming useful across a lot of fields, but progress won’t look the same everywhere. In software, you can generate code, run it, and get feedback quickly. In science or medicine, a promising idea might still need an experiment or a clinical study, so the path from a model’s output to a real breakthrough is longer.

A lot depends on getting these tools into the hands of people who really understand their domain. They know which questions matter, and they can tell when an answer that sounds convincing is actually missing something. So I’d expect breakthroughs to spread through that interaction: better models enable experts to try new things, and those experts reveal what the models need to get better at.

r001.rationale: The response says AI is becoming useful across many fields and progress varies by field, but it does not characterize advances across nearly every profession as “Move 37”-like breakthroughs.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s going to be uneven. In some fields, you can test an idea quickly and get a clear signal about whether it works. Coding is a good example: you can run the code, run the tests, and iterate. That creates a really fast feedback loop.

Other fields have longer feedback cycles. If you’re developing a drug, having a promising hypothesis is valuable, but you still have to do the experiments. So the pace of AI progress and the pace of real-world impact can look quite different.

What I’m excited about is giving people across those fields more ability to explore ideas. You still need domain expertise to ask the right questions and judge the results, but the cost of trying something can come down substantially.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI progress as uneven across fields and contrasts coding’s fast feedback with drug development’s longer cycle; it does not characterize advances across nearly every field as “Move 37”-like breakthroughs.

r002.rationale: The response says AI can lower the cost of exploring ideas, while noting the need for domain expertise. It does not state that AI agents can perform long-horizon work in people’s professions.
